ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The NECS and LCCP studies were approved by the institutional review board at Boston University Medical Campus.
The ILO and RADCO studies were approved by the single institutional review board at Albert Einstein College of Medicine.

RADCO participants are identified from ongoing studies of centenarians and their offspring (UH3AG064704: The Integrative Longevity Omics Study and U19AG023122: the Centenarian Project of the Longevity Consortium) and are classified into cognitive superagers, individuals whose performance on memory tasks matches normative expectations for persons ~30 years younger, and individuals with average-cognition.

The Resilience/Resistance to Alzheimer's Disease in Centenarians and Offspring (RADCO) eligible participants are identified from ongoing studies of centenarians and their offspring (UH3AG064704: The Integrative Longevity Omics Study and U19AG023122: the Centenarian Project of the Longevity Consortium).

Participants were enrolled in the New England Centenarian Study (NECS), Longevity Consortium Centenarian Project (LCCP), Integrative Longevity Omics (ILO), and/or the Resilience/Resistance to Alzheimer's Disease in Centenarians and Offspring Study (RADCO).
All participants or their legally authorized representatives provided written informed consent.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> RADCO participants are identified from ongoing studies of centenarians and their offspring (UH3AG064704: The Integrative Longevity Omics Study and U19AG023122: the Centenarian Project of the Longevity Consortium) and are classified into cognitive superagers, individuals whose performance on memory tasks matches normative expectations for persons ~30 years younger, and individuals with average-cognition.

> The Resilience/Resistance to Alzheimer's Disease in Centenarians and Offspring (RADCO) eligible participants are identified from ongoing studies of centenarians and their offspring (UH3AG064704: The Integrative Longevity Omics Study and U19AG023122: the Centenarian Project of the Longevity Consortium).

> Participants were enrolled in the New England Centenarian Study (NECS), Longevity Consortium Centenarian Project (LCCP), Integrative Longevity Omics (ILO), and/or the Resilience/Resistance to Alzheimer's Disease in Centenarians and Offspring Study (RADCO).

> All participants or their legally authorized representatives provided written informed consent.

Ethics approval statement:

> The NECS and LCCP studies were approved by the institutional review board at Boston University Medical Campus.

> The ILO and RADCO studies were approved by the single institutional review board at Albert Einstein College of Medicine.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P = 0.43", "P > 0.01"), Sentence = c("The candidate missense-to-synonymous ratio (1.45:1) did not significantly differ from that of the 870,018 frequency-matched rare exonic variants in the same cohort (1.59:1; OR = 0.91, Fisher's exact P = 0.43), indicating that the functional-class composition of the candidate set is typical of rare exonic variation; full details on this analysis are in Supplementary Table Restricting candidates to moderate-to-high predicted impact and excluding singlelineage or Hardy-Weinberg-deviating variants and completing our variant filtering pipeline as described in Figure 3 yielded 114 significant candidates, full details in Supplementary Table B5.", "Variants were retained only if they demonstrated a statistically significant difference in allele frequency via Fisher's exact test between the RADCO cognitive superager group and the gnomAD NFE reference population (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted Fisher's exact P < 0.01) while simultaneously showing no significant difference between the RADCO average-cognition group and gnomAD NFE (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted Fisher's exact P > 0.01)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

ethics_statements: The NECS and LCCP studies were approved by the institutional review board at Boston University Medical Campus.
The ILO and RADCO studies were approved by the single institutional review board at Albert Einstein College of Medicine.
live_data_statements: RADCO participants are identified from ongoing studies of centenarians and their offspring (UH3AG064704: The Integrative Longevity Omics Study and U19AG023122: the Centenarian Project of the Longevity Consortium) and are classified into cognitive superagers, individuals whose performance on memory tasks matches normative expectations for persons ~30 years younger, and individuals with average-cognition.

The Resilience/Resistance to Alzheimer's Disease in Centenarians and Offspring (RADCO) eligible participants are identified from ongoing studies of centenarians and their offspring (UH3AG064704: The Integrative Longevity Omics Study and U19AG023122: the Centenarian Project of the Longevity Consortium).

Participants were enrolled in the New England Centenarian Study (NECS), Longevity Consortium Centenarian Project (LCCP), Integrative Longevity Omics (ILO), and/or the Resilience/Resistance to Alzheimer's Disease in Centenarians and Offspring Study (RADCO).
All participants or their legally authorized representatives provided written informed consent.
